description: Space Alpha builds Mispriced Winters: weather derivatives are often priced by averaging past winters, but winters keep getting warmer, so those prices overstate the cold. We use NASA POWER temperatures to find the warming trend, measure its cost in dollars and test it with a backtest. A working Python app is already built. We’re looking for Python/data skills, stats or quant finance, data viz, and pitch/demo design. Want to actively build? Send a join request.
details:
What it does. Weather futures and options settle on degree-day indices. Each day’s average temperature, (Tmax + Tmin) / 2, is compared with a base of 65 °F (the US exchange convention) or 18 °C. Heating degree days (HDD) count how much colder the day was, and cooling degree days (CDD) how much warmer. A common way to price these contracts is burn analysis: it averages what a contract would have paid over the last 10–20 seasons, which quietly assumes the climate isn’t changing. Mispriced Winters measures how wrong that assumption is, city by city and contract by contract, in dollars.

Data. The app downloads daily maximum and minimum 2-metre air temperatures from 1981 to today from the NASA POWER Daily API. POWER is built on NASA’s MERRA-2 reanalysis, which uses a grid of roughly 50 km. The app covers 18 preset cities (8 in the US with exchange rules, 5 in Europe and 5 in Ukraine) plus any coordinates the user enters, and it saves downloads locally.

Trend detection. For every season the app computes the contract index: winter HDD (November–March), single winter months, or summer CDD (May–September, July, August). It estimates the trend with the Theil–Sen slope and tests it with the Mann–Kendall test, using the Hamed–Rao correction for autocorrelation. The Benjamini–Hochberg procedure controls false discoveries across all 18 cities.

Pricing. The same call or put is priced three ways:

  1. Naive burn analysis.
  2. Trend-adjusted burn: every historical day is shifted into the target season’s climate using the detected warming rate.
  3. An independent daily temperature model with seasonal harmonics, a trend and AR(p) dynamics, simulated with 5,000 Monte Carlo paths and bootstrapped shocks.

The gap between (1) and (2) is the mispricing, in dollars per contract and in percent. (3) is an independent check.

Validation. A walk-forward backtest re-prices every season since 2001 using only data available before that season started, then compares the forecast with what happened. It answers two questions: is the naive forecast biased, and how much would a buyer paying the naive price have lost compared with one paying the adjusted price?

Interface. The app has four tabs:

  • Overview: a warming map and a ranking of all cities
  • City case file: the four detective answers, the three prices and charts
  • Backtest
  • Method: formulas, sources and limitations

Users can change the contract, strike, tick size, cap, discount rate, length of history and model settings.

Benefits and intended impact. Hedgers such as energy companies, utilities, farmers and insurers can see whether they’re paying for cold that no longer comes. Traders and risk managers get a testable estimate of how much a climate trend moves a price. Ukrainian cities, where energy and agriculture depend heavily on weather, get the same analysis as exchange-listed US cities. The project also makes climate change concrete for non-scientists: not just “+0.5 °C per decade”, but “this contract is overpriced by X dollars”.

Tools. Python, pandas, NumPy, SciPy, Plotly, Streamlit and Requests. No special hardware is needed; it runs on a laptop. We used an SI assistant, Claude by Anthropic, to brainstorm the idea, generate most of the code, and draft the slides. This is noted in the README.

What makes it creative. Climate trend analysis usually stops once the trend is found. We connect it to a market: the statistics that detect a trend become an input to an option price, and the backtest shows whether acting on the trend would have paid off. Pricing one contract three independent ways lets users see which method is wrong instead of trusting a single model. The app also covers Ukrainian cities, which have no exchange-listed weather contracts, as hypothetical contracts.

Factors we considered.

  • Honest validation: the backtest never uses future data, and the multiple-testing correction stops us from “discovering” trends by chance across 18 cities.
  • Exchange conventions: the daily average comes from the max and min, US cities use a 65 °F base, contracts pay $20 per degree day, and seasons follow the standard windows.
  • Data limits: a ~50 km reanalysis grid cell is not the weather station a contract settles on (basis risk). Also, POWER’s daily max/min may not match a station’s measurement day. Results should therefore be checked against station data such as NOAA GHCN-Daily.
  • Model scope: prices are actuarial (expected payoff, optionally discounted) and include no market risk premium. The trend is linear, and seasonal forecasts (ENSO, NAO) aren’t included yet.
  • Data quality: gaps of up to 3 days are filled, and incomplete seasons are left out.
